questions.q: Define the three main structural stages of a formal interview text and state the purpose of each stage in one sentence.
questions.a: The three stages are: (1) Opening/Introduction — establishes rapport, introduces the interviewee, and sets context with low-stakes factual questions; (2) Body/Development — explores experiences, challenges, turning points through probing and open-ended questions; (3) Closing/Conclusion — synthesises insights, looks forward, and ends on an inspirational or reflective note. A wrong answer that lists "beginning, middle, end" without linking each to question purpose shows the student sees structure as arbitrary rather than functional.

questions.q: In the textbook interview with Dr. Deepa Malik, the interviewer asks: "You were diagnosed with a spinal tumour at age 29. How did that moment change your life's direction?" Identify the question type and explain why it is placed in the middle of the interview, not at the start.
questions.a: This is a probing, open-ended question targeting a turning point. It appears mid-interview because the opening has built trust with easier questions; placing it earlier would feel intrusive and might elicit a guarded response. A wrong answer calling it just "a difficult question" misses the strategic sequencing — the student hasn't grasped that interview structure manages emotional safety to elicit depth.

questions.q:
Given this interview excerpt:  
Q: "What sports did you play as a child?"  
A: "I loved cricket and swimming."  
Q: "When did you first realise you wanted to compete professionally?"  
A: "After my accident, when I discovered para-sports."  
Identify the shift in question focus and explain its effect on the narrative arc.
questions.a: The shift is from factual/background (childhood sports) to motivational/turning point (professional aspiration post-accident). This moves the narrative from "who she was" to "who she became," creating a transformation arc. A student who only notes "first question easy, second harder" misses the thematic pivot — the interview is structuring a journey from ability to disability to renewed possibility.

questions.q:
Compare these two closing questions from different interviews:  
(A) "Any final words for our readers?"  
(B) "Looking at India's para-sports ecosystem today, what single change would you fight for?"  
Analyse which better serves a board exam answer about the theme "Redefining Possibilities" and why.
questions.a: Question (B) is superior for thematic analysis because it elicits a specific, forward-looking stance on systemic change — directly supporting "Redefining Possibilities" with concrete vision. Question (A) yields generic platitudes. A student choosing (A) reveals they confuse "closing question" with "any last question" rather than seeing the closing as a thematic anchor.

questions.q: A Class 9 student writes this analysis: "The interview uses many questions to get information. The interviewer asks about Deepa's childhood, then her accident, then her medals. This shows her life story." Evaluate this response for board exam adequacy. What is missing?
questions.a: The response is inadequate: it summarises content but analyses nothing. Missing: (1) identification of question types, (2) explanation of sequencing strategy, (3) connection between structure and theme (resilience/redefinition), (4) textual evidence with PEEL structure. A student producing this thinks "analysis" means "retell in order" — a middle-school habit not broken for board-level demand.

questions.q: Design three interview questions for a para-athlete that would structurally mirror the textbook interview's arc: one opening, one turning-point, one closing. Label each with its stage and question type.
questions.a:
Opening: "What's your earliest memory of playing sport?" (Factual, rapport-building)  
Turning-point: "The 2016 Rio Paralympics — take us to the moment you realised you'd won silver. What went through your mind?" (Probing, emotional, pivotal moment)  
Closing: "If you could change one perception about disability in Indian sports tomorrow, what would it be?" (Visionary, thematic, forward-looking)  
A poor answer uses three factual questions or random order — showing no internalised structural template.
